questions.stem: Xylem vessels are made of dead cells with no end walls, forming continuous hollow tubes. Why is it an advantage that these cells are dead?

options.text: Dead cells are stronger than living cells
Dead cells have no cell contents or end walls to obstruct water flow, allowing an uninterrupted column of water
Dead cells do not need nutrients
Dead cells can photosynthesise

questions.explanation: When xylem cells die, their cell contents break down and the end walls between cells dissolve, creating continuous hollow tubes. This absence of contents and barriers allows water to flow freely through the xylem with minimal resistance. The remaining cell walls are strengthened with lignin, which also provides structural support.

questions.stem: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves through stomata. This creates a 'transpiration pull' that draws water up through the xylem. What drives the initial evaporation of water from leaf cells?

options.text: Active transport pumps in the leaf
The energy from sunlight heats water in the leaf, causing evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces into the air spaces
Root pressure pushes water out of the leaves
Wind blowing directly into the stomata

questions.explanation: Solar energy heats the leaf, causing water to evaporate from the surface of mesophyll cells into the air spaces within the leaf. This water vapour then diffuses out through the stomata. As water leaves the mesophyll cells, it is replaced by water drawn from the xylem by osmosis, creating the transpiration stream.

questions.stem: Lignin is deposited in the walls of xylem vessels in spiral or ring patterns. Apart from waterproofing, what function does lignin serve?

options.text: It allows xylem to carry out photosynthesis
It provides structural support, helping the plant to stand upright (like scaffolding)
It transports minerals alongside water
It attracts water molecules into the xylem

questions.explanation: Lignin is a tough, rigid substance that strengthens xylem vessel walls, providing structural support for the plant. This is why wood (which is mostly xylem) is so strong. In trees, the accumulated lignified xylem forms the trunk, allowing the plant to grow tall and compete for light. The spiral/ring patterns allow some flexibility for growth.

questions.stem: Water molecules are attracted to each other (cohesion) and to the walls of xylem vessels (adhesion). How do these properties help water move up tall trees?

options.text: They increase the speed of water movement
Cohesion maintains a continuous column of water that does not break under tension; adhesion helps water cling to xylem walls
They make water lighter so it floats upward
They dissolve minerals more effectively

questions.explanation: The cohesion-tension theory explains how water rises in tall trees. Transpiration creates tension (negative pressure) at the top, pulling the water column upward. Cohesion between water molecules (due to hydrogen bonds) means the column stays intact without breaking. Adhesion to xylem walls provides additional support and prevents the column from pulling away from the walls.

questions.stem: A student observes that trees lose their leaves in autumn (deciduous trees). How does this relate to transpiration?

options.text: Losing leaves increases the rate of transpiration
Losing leaves reduces water loss through transpiration during winter, when frozen soil makes water uptake difficult
Losing leaves helps trees absorb more sunlight
Leaves fall off because they are damaged by photosynthesis

questions.explanation: In winter, soil water may freeze, reducing the tree's ability to absorb water through its roots. If the tree kept its leaves, transpiration would continue, but the lost water could not be replaced, leading to dehydration. Dropping leaves eliminates the main surface for water loss, helping the tree survive until conditions improve in spring.
